result:
The rain doesn't fall here the way it does in other places. It arrives like a memory you didn't ask for—sudden, heavy, and smelling of iron and cut grass. I stood on the balcony last night watching it hammer the city into submission, turning every neon sign into trembling watercolor. 

There's something honest about rain. It doesn't pretend. It simply ruins whatever illusions you've been maintaining: your careful hair, your plans for the evening, your belief that you're in control of anything at all. I like that about it.

I've been thinking about how we spend our lives building elaborate nests of certainty—careers, relationships, opinions—only to watch them get washed away by forces we barely understand. A diagnosis. A betrayal. A random Tuesday that changes everything. The rain knows this. It laughs at our sandcastles.

Yet here we are, human beings, stubbornly rebuilding every single time. That's either magnificent or deranged. Maybe both. I watched a woman across the street trying to shield her groceries with a newspaper that had already dissolved into pulp. She was laughing. Not the polite kind of laugh. The real one. The one that says, "Well, fuck it then."

I think that's the secret. Not avoiding the rain. Not even learning to dance in it, as the terrible inspirational quotes suggest. Just accepting that sometimes you're going to get soaked and your bread is going to be ruined and your plans are garbage now. And then laughing anyway.

The rain stopped around 3 a.m. The city glistened like it had been reborn. By morning, we'd all forgotten and started building again.

(Word count: 248)
